@graph.headline: How Many Trades to Validate a Trading Strategy? The Evidence Contract

acceptedAnswer.text: Three tiers: ~100 trades is an early hypothesis, 200–500 supports a serious risk decision, and 1,000+ is needed to prove a small edge (a 0.08R-per-trade edge with 1R noise needs roughly 1,200 trades before it's statistically visible). But the count only works if the trades are independent and span different market regimes.

mainEntity.name: How many trades do I need to backtest for valid results?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — 30 trades is a pattern-spotter, not a verdict. A true 50% win rate prints anywhere from ~32% to ~68% over 30 trades at 95% confidence, on variance alone. The same thin sample feeds two opposite mistakes: believing a lucky 68% is an edge, or quitting a working strategy during a normal losing streak.

mainEntity.name: Is 30 trades enough to judge a strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the trades are independent and rule-following. Two hundred scalps taken on one trend day share one market condition — they're one observation wearing a 200-trade costume. Regime coverage (trending, ranging, volatile, quiet) is part of what makes a sample genuinely "big."

mainEntity.name: Does a bigger sample always mean more certainty?

acceptedAnswer.text: At 2–4 trades a month, roughly 2–4 years of history. The practical answer: backtest supplies the history (an honest manual or automated backtest across regimes), then forward-test the last 30–50 trades on paper to confirm the edge survives your execution. Sample size is denominated in trades, not months.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take a swing trader to get 100 trades?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your edge has a size and your sample has a count; power asks whether the count is big enough to notice the size. The one-line math: t = (average trade result) ÷ (noise per trade ÷ √n). Bigger edge → fewer trades needed; bigger noise → more. Small edges whisper — you have to listen longer.

mainEntity.name: What is statistical power in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the required sample grows with the inverse square of the edge: t = edge × √n ÷ noise. Halve the edge, quadruple the trades. And Indian F&O costs shrink the after-cost edge — brokerage, STT, exchange charges, slippage — so costs don't just take your profit, they multiply the evidence burden.

mainEntity.name: Why do I need MORE trades if my edge is small?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A t-test asks "did this sample make money?", not "did the strategy predict anything?" A recent trading-statistics experiment ran thousands of simulated markets with nothing predictable and found naive t-tests cried "edge" far more often than their promised 5% rate in some market shapes — while a shuffled-placebo test stayed honest. Passing a t-test is not proof of prediction.

mainEntity.name: Does a t-test prove my strategy has an edge?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every tweak after seeing results spends some of the sample's credibility — testing 11 variations and keeping the best is 11 tests, not 1 (at a nominal 5% bar, ~43% chance at least one false positive). Keep tweaks to a minimum and lock rules before testing. The full treatment — multiple-testing corrections and the parameter-cliff test — lives in the overfitting chapter.
